lines: In my younger and more weak years my father gave me some suggestions that I've been turning over in my consciousness ever since.
``Whenever you feel like criticising any one,'' he told me, ``just remember that all the people in this planet haven't had the privileges that you've had.''

He didn't say any more, but we've always been unusually open in a quiet path, and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence, I'm inclined to reserve all judgments, a practice that has opened up many odd natures to me and also made me the casualty of not a few seasoned bores. The unusual mind is prompt to detect and attach itself to this quality when it appears in a normal person, and so it came about that in academy I was unjustly accused of being a politician, because I was privy to the secret griefs of wild, strange men. Most of the confidences were unwanted---frequently I have feigned sleep, preoccupation, or a aggressive playfulness when I realized by some unmistakable signal that an close revelation was quivering on the horizon; for the confidential epiphanies of fresh men, or at least the periods in which they express them, are usually unoriginal and marred by manifest repressions. Reserving verdicts is a matter of endless aspiration. I am still a little afraid of missing something if I forget that, as my father snobbishly suggested, and I snobbishly repeat, a sense of the underlying civilities is parcelled out unequally at birth.

And, after boasting this path of my tolerance, I come to the acknowledgment that it has a limit. Deportment may be founded on the hard rock or the wet bogs, but after a certain point I don't care what it's founded on. When I came back from the East last autumn I felt that I wanted the society to be in uniform and at a sort of moral focus eternally; I wanted no more chaotic journeys with privileged glimpses into the human centre. Only Gatsby, the man who gives his name to this book, was exempt from my attentiveness---Gatsby, who represented everything for which I have an unaffected contempt. If mood is an unbroken chain of winning gestures, then there was something stunning about him, some elevated attentiveness to the guarantees of life, as if he were related to one of those elaborate mechanisms that register earthquakes ten thousand miles away. This responsiveness had nothing to do with that feeble influence which is dignified under the name of the ``artistic personality''---it was an remarkable gift for confidence, a loving readiness such as I have never found in any other person and which it is not likely I shall ever find again. No---Gatsby turned out all right at the end; it is what preyed on Gatsby, what filthy powder floated in the wake of his ambitions that temporarily closed out my interest in the futile sorrows and short-winded excitement of men.

My clan have been distinguished, well-to-do people in this Centre Western city for three generations. The Carraways are something of a lineage, and we have a tradition that we're descended from the Dukes of Buccleuch, but the true founder of my line was my grandfather's brother, who came here in fifty-single, sent a substitute to the Civil War, and started the wholesale hardware corporation that my father carries on to-day.

I never saw this great-uncle, but I'm supposed to look like him---with special citation to the rather hard-boiled canvas that hangs in father's office. I graduated from Youthful Haven in 1915, just a quarter of a century after my father, and a little later I participated in that delayed Teutonic relocation known as the Great War. I enjoyed the counter-raid so thoroughly that I came back anxious. Instead of being the mild heart of the globe, the Middle West now seemed like the rough border of the universe---so I decided to go East and learn the bond corporation. Everybody I knew was in the bond organization, so I supposed it could support sole more solitary man. All my aunts and uncles talked it over as if they were choosing a prep college for me, and finally said, ``Why---ye-es,'' with very grave, tentative faces. Father agreed to finance me for a year, and after multiple holdups I came East, eternally, I plan, in the spring of twenty-two.

The realistic thing was to find compartments in the city, but it was a mild period, and I had just left a territory of expansive lawns and amiable trees, so when a young man at the office suggested that we take a abode together in a commuting town, it sounded like a great concept. He found the house, a deteriorated cardboard bungalow at eighty a month, but at the last minute the business ordered him to Washington, and I went out to the region alone. I had a dog---at least I had him for a few days until he ran away---and an old Dodge and a Finnish woman, who made my bed and cooked breakfast and muttered Finnish knowledge to herself over the energized stove.
It was lonely for a day or so until individual morning some man, more recently arrived than I, stopped me on the highway.
``How do you get to West Egg town?'' he asked helplessly.
I told him. And as I walked on I was lonely no longer. I was a guide, a scout, an initial colonist. He had casually conferred on me the freedom of the neighborhood.
